services</a></nav></aside><article class="reading-body"><section class="reading-section" id="start"><h2>Start with the hours when your sign needs to work.</h2><p>A shop sign should help customers recognise the business and find the entrance. Whether it needs illumination depends on the setting and trading pattern, not simply on whether lighting looks impressive in a photograph. A daytime showroom on a well-lit parade has a different brief from a restaurant welcoming customers after dark. Consider the approach from both directions and the points at which people make decisions.</p><p>Photograph the frontage in daylight and after dark before choosing. Include neighbouring signs, nearby windows and the entrance itself. This helps separate a branding problem from a lighting problem. If the name is too small or visually crowded, adding light may make the same weak layout brighter without making the business easier to identify.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="at-a-glance"><h2>Compare at a glance.</h2><p class="table-hint">On a smaller screen, scroll across to compare all options.</p><div aria-label="Illuminated vs non-illuminated shop signs comparison table" class="comparison-scroll" role="region" tabindex="0"><table><caption>Illuminated vs non-illuminated shop signs at a glance</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Factor</th><th scope="col">Illuminated sign</th><th scope="col">Non-illuminated sign</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">After-dark identity</th><td>Designed light can support recognition</td><td>Depends on available ambient light</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Daytime appearance</th><td>Assess materials with lights switched off</td><td>Assess colour, shape and depth</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Installation</th><td>Includes lighting and electrical coordination</td><td>Primarily fabrication and mounting</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Maintenance</th><td>Access needed for lighting components</td><td>Cleaning and fixing checks still needed</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Operating cost</th><td>Depends on power, hours and tariff</td><td>No sign-lighting energy requirement</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Design flexibility</th><td>Construction affects fine detail and effects</td><td>Printed or cut details offer different options</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Neighbours</th><td>Consider brightness and operating hours</td><td>Consider scale, colour and frontage impact</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Permissions</th><td>Check actual lighting and site proposal</td><td>Do not assume an automatic exemption</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Best starting point</th><td>Evening recognition or a defined lighting brief</td><td>Daytime identity and a simpler sign system</td></tr></tbody></table></div></section><section class="reading-section" id="lit"><h2>Illuminated signs: useful visibility with more to coordinate.</h2><p>Illumination can be incorporated in different ways. Face-lit letters direct light through the letter faces; halo lighting creates an effect behind lettering; external lighting can illuminate a sign face from outside. Fabricated letters can be specified with different illuminated options to suit the design. These approaches should be compared through actual samples and a frontage design.</p><p>Lighting is worth exploring when your entrance needs recognition during evening trading, when the surrounding environment is visually busy or when the design calls for a particular night-time identity. The result depends on the letter shape, colour, mounting background and viewing angle. A restrained, readable scheme can be more effective than lighting every graphic element.</p><p>The additional considerations include an electrical supply, cable routing, access to equipment and a maintenance plan. Ask where drivers or other components will sit and how they can be reached later. A beautiful initial installation can be inconvenient to service if access is hidden behind permanent finishes. Confirm responsibilities for electrical work before the fit-out schedule is fixed.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="unlit"><h2>Non-illuminated signs: strong branding with a simpler system.</h2><p>A non-illuminated sign can still have a distinctive, premium appearance. Materials, colour contrast, depth and spacing all contribute. Flat panels, fabricated trays and raised lettering give different design options without requiring lighting within the sign. Daytime businesses may find that a carefully composed non-illuminated fascia meets the brief very well.</p><p>The main limit is how the sign will be seen when ambient light falls. Street lighting or nearby shop windows should not be assumed to provide reliable, even illumination of your frontage. If night-time recognition matters, inspect the actual location after dark. Look at the name from the pavement and from the normal customer approach rather than standing directly underneath it.</p><p>An unlit sign still needs cleaning, sound fixings and a planned installation. It is not maintenance-free, and choosing it does not automatically remove advertisement-consent questions. Its simpler construction can reduce the number of systems to coordinate, but the mounting surface and the intended appearance remain important parts of the quotation.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="design"><h2>Judge the daytime and evening appearance together.</h2><p>A sign that glows attractively at night also has to represent the business during daylight. Ask how the face materials and returns will look when switched off. Conversely, a dark printed brand colour may behave differently when translated into a translucent illuminated face. Agree how closely the design needs to match other brand applications and review samples where that distinction matters.</p><p>Keep lettering legible before adding decorative effects. Fine strokes, tightly spaced characters and complicated symbols can be difficult to translate into some illuminated constructions. A secondary strapline may work better as a simpler element beneath the main name. The aim is a clear hierarchy that suits the frontage, not forcing every part of the logo into the same construction.</p><p>Consider neighbouring premises and residential windows. Discuss the intended operating hours, brightness control and switching arrangements from the outset. Avoid specifying a permanently bright display simply because a control decision has been postponed. The selected scheme should be comfortable in its surroundings as well as useful to your customers.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="cost"><h2>Compare the whole project and its upkeep.</h2><p>The purchase price alone does not describe an illuminated sign. A complete comparison should identify fabrication, fitting, access equipment, electrical work, any alterations to the frontage and commissioning. Ask whether the quotation includes removing the old sign and making good visible areas. An apparently inexpensive option may exclude work that another supplier has included.</p><p>Running cost depends on the installed power requirement, operating hours and your electricity tariff. Ask for the actual specification rather than using a generic estimate for all LED signs. Maintenance costs depend partly on how accessible the installation is. A component above an awkward canopy presents a different service task from one designed with straightforward access.</p><p>For both options, ask what is covered by the agreed warranty and what maintenance the owner should arrange. Keep the approved drawing, material details and any electrical documentation. If the business later changes hours, branding or occupancy, those records make it easier to understand what can be retained and what needs redesigning.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="consent"><h2>Confirm permissions for the actual design.</h2><p>In England, advertisement control is a separate consent regime. Some signs have deemed consent subject to conditions; others require express consent. Illumination, position and the building context can affect the assessment. A non-illuminated sign is not automatically exempt. Refer to <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">GOV.UK advertisement guidance</a> and check the specific proposal with the local planning authority before manufacture.</p><p>Landlord approval is a separate matter, and listed buildings may require additional consent. For a useful initial enquiry, provide dimensions, a frontage photograph and a description of the proposed lighting and hours. Our <a href="/signage-home/guides-and-advice/planning-consent-for-shop-signs">shop-sign consent guide</a> helps you prepare that information. The final requirements come from the relevant authority and the circumstances of the site.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="scenarios"><h2>Examples of when each approach earns its place.</h2><p>Illustrative example: a restaurant operates into the evening on a street with competing illuminated frontages. A clearly readable illuminated name could help customers locate it, but the solution should be tested against the neighbouring windows and the entrance lighting. Lighting the principal name may be enough; a long list of services need not glow too.</p><p>Illustrative example: a daytime interiors showroom has a generous fascia and a strong, simple wordmark. Non-illuminated raised lettering or a well-finished panel could provide the desired identity. The budget may be better spent on proportion, materials and installation than on a lighting system the business does not need during normal customer visits.</p><p>Illustrative example: a small professional practice occupies a sensitive frontage. A restrained unlit design might be a useful option to discuss with the landlord and authority. That is a design starting point, not a promise of approval. The building details and proposed fixings still need consideration.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="next"><h2>Make the decision with a frontage proposal.</h2><p>Bring the comparison back to one drawing of your actual premises. Show the sign dimensions, lettering, background, fittings and any lighting locations. Review it at the intended reading distance, then compare what changes between the lit and unlit options. This makes the discussion practical and helps avoid spending on features that do not improve recognition or the customer journey.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Business opening hours and when customers arrive after dark.</li><li>Frontage photographs in daylight and after dark.</li><li>Sign dimensions, mounting height and proposed reading distance.</li><li>Logo files and any important brand colour requirements.</li><li>Known electrical supply, access constraints and fit-out dates.</li><li>Landlord requirements, listed status or existing consent documents.</li><li>Budget for fabrication, installation and ongoing maintenance.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. Answered.</h2><details><summary>Are all illuminated signs very bright?</summary><p>No. Effects vary with construction, material, light output and controls. Discuss the required appearance and the surroundings. Ask to review a relevant sample rather than assuming every illuminated sign will resemble a bright lightbox.</p></details><details><summary>Can lighting be added later?</summary><p>Sometimes, but it should not be assumed. The structure, materials, electrical provision and permissions may need reconsideration. If future lighting is likely, mention it during the original design so the options can be assessed.</p></details><details><summary>Will an illuminated sign increase enquiries?</summary><p>It may improve recognition in the right setting, but there is no guaranteed sales result. Good positioning, readable design and an obvious entrance remain essential. Choose lighting to solve a specific visibility need.</p></details><details><summary>Who decides whether consent is needed?</summary><p>The local planning authority can advise on the actual proposal. Provide dimensions, position and lighting details. Landlord permission and any other site-specific approvals should be addressed separately.</p></details></section><section class="reading-section" id="sources"><h2>Sources & further reading.</h2><p class="source-note">Sources checked for this draft on 18 October 2026. Product ratings apply to the stated product and test conditions; confirm the current specification for your order.</p><ul class="source-links"><li><a class="" href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">Advertisement guidance for England ↗</a></li></ul></section><section class="reading-section" id="services"><h2>Put the advice into practice.</h2><p>Tell us where the sign will go, what it needs to communicate and the date you are working towards. Our Norwich team can discuss the design, materials and fitting around your project.</p><div class="service-links"><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs">Illuminated signs ↗</a><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs">Fascia signs ↗</a></div><p><a class="" href="/signage-home/signage-norwich">Visit our Norwich workshop ↗</a> · <a class="" href="/sectors">Find signage for your sector ↗</a></p></section></article></div><section class="section tint"><div class="wrap"><h2>A little more guidance.</h2><div class="grid research-cards"><article class="card" data-search="Built-up letters vs flat panel signs Decide whether your frontage needs dimensional lettering, a continuous branded face or a combination. </style><div class="crmseo-d crmseo-html"><div class="brand"><div class="research-hero wrap"><span class="eyebrow">Compare your options</span><h1>PVC vs mesh banners</h1><p>A solid banner gives you a continuous print surface. Mesh introduces openings that change both the graphic and the installation conversation. Choose around the position, exposure and message.</p><a class="button white" href="#enquiry">DISCUSS YOUR SIGNAGE ↗</a></div></div><div class="research-hero-image wrap"><img alt="PVC vs mesh banners — signage example" fetchpriority="high" height="900" loading="eager" src="https://dipjypzrfigkzuarlsov.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/seo-images/ae4393de-99e2-4a0f-be28-2866e44443bd/signage/research/pvc-vs-mesh-banners.webp" width="1600"/></div><nav aria-label="Breadcrumb" class="crumb wrap"><a class="" href="/signage-home/compare">Comparisons ↗</a> / <span aria-current="page">PVC vs mesh banners</span></nav><nav aria-label="Signage advice sections" class="research-tabs wrap"><a class="active" href="/signage-home/compare">Comparisons ↗</a><a class="" href="/signage-home/guides-and-advice">Guides & advice ↗</a></nav><main><div class="wrap reading-layout"><aside class="article-toc"><nav aria-label="Article contents"><h2>In this comparison</h2><a href="#start">The important difference is solid versus open-weave.</a><a href="#at-a-glance">Compare at a glance</a><a href="#solid">Solid PVC: give the printed message a continuous background.</a><a href="#mesh">Mesh: useful where the openings serve a purpose.</a><a href="#finishing">Hems, eyelets and pockets need an installation plan.</a><a href="#design">Design for the background and approach.</a><a href="#scenarios">Three examples of how the brief changes the choice.</a><a href="#permissions">Check the position before committing to production.</a><a href="#care">Plan handling, inspection and the next campaign.</a><a href="#checklist">What to send us</a><a href="#faq">Questions & answers</a><a href="#sources">Sources & further reading</a><a href="#services">Explore the services</a></nav></aside><article class="reading-body"><section class="reading-section" id="start"><h2>The important difference is solid versus open-weave.</h2><p>People often ask for PVC or mesh as if these were two completely different material families. In practice, many mesh banners are also PVC-coated. The useful comparison is between a solid printed banner and a perforated or open-weave mesh banner. For example, <a href="https://www.hexis-graphics.com/en/produit/pg450/">HEXIS PG450</a> is described by its manufacturer as a PVC-coated polyester mesh. Always compare the exact products offered rather than relying on the shorthand name.</p><p>The choice starts with the installation. A sheltered wall display, an exposed fence and a large scaffold advertisement present very different conditions. Mesh openings can let air pass through, but they do not make the banner windproof or remove the load on its supports. Tell us what the graphic will attach to before deciding the material, finished size or finishing method.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="at-a-glance"><h2>Compare at a glance.</h2><p class="table-hint">On a smaller screen, scroll across to compare all options.</p><div aria-label="PVC vs mesh banners comparison table" class="comparison-scroll" role="region" tabindex="0"><table><caption>PVC vs mesh banners at a glance</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Factor</th><th scope="col">Solid PVC banner</th><th scope="col">Mesh banner</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Print surface</th><td>Continuous face for artwork</td><td>Open structure affects appearance</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Wind exposure</th><td>Requires suitable supports and assessment</td><td>Openings help air pass; assessment still needed</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Close-up detail</th><td>Useful for fine design where viewing allows</td><td>Simplify small text and intricate features</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Background</th><td>Usually more visually continuous</td><td>Background can show through openings</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Privacy</th><td>Discuss opacity of exact product</td><td>Do not assume privacy or concealment</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Fixing</th><td>Specify hems, eyelets or pockets</td><td>Specify compatible reinforcement and fixing</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Double-sided display</th><td>Requires an appropriate product and layout</td><td>Do not assume readable artwork on both sides</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Best starting point</th><td>Sheltered promotions and continuous graphics</td><td>Selected exposed or large-format applications</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Structural approval</th><td>Needed for the actual support arrangement</td><td>Not avoided by choosing mesh</td></tr></tbody></table></div></section><section class="reading-section" id="solid"><h2>Solid PVC: give the printed message a continuous background.</h2><p>A solid banner is useful when you want broad colour, photography or text to sit on an uninterrupted surface. It is a natural option to compare for promotions, event announcements and temporary branding where the position and support suit it. Because the face is continuous, the design does not have to work around the visual effect of open mesh.</p><p>Its limitation is also its defining feature: the solid face presents a larger continuous area to moving air. A banner must not be treated as an ordinary poster when it is fixed outdoors. The condition and strength of the structure, the attachment method and the exposure need to be assessed together. A convenient fence is not automatically a suitable structure.</p><p>Discuss whether the display needs to be read from one or both sides. Standard front-facing banner construction should not be assumed to provide an effective double-sided graphic. If people approach from opposite directions, a different specification or two separately planned displays may be more appropriate. Tell us whether sunlight or lighting behind the banner could affect the presentation.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="mesh"><h2>Mesh: useful where the openings serve a purpose.</h2><p>Mesh is worth considering for some exposed outdoor positions and large displays because its open structure allows some air and light through. The amount depends on the actual weave and product specification. Avoid choosing from an unsupported percentage claim: the whole installation still has to be appropriate for the site.</p><p>Those openings also remove parts of the printable surface. A graphic can look different against a pale wall, an open yard or a busy background visible through it. Strong shapes, clear text and a restrained message are useful starting points. A tiny address or intricate pattern that looks crisp on screen may not deliver the same result when printed on mesh and viewed at a distance.</p><p>Mesh is not a privacy screen simply because it carries artwork. If hiding activity behind a fence is part of the brief, make that requirement explicit. Equally, a banner cannot be assumed to provide a certified containment or safety function. Advertising, screening and protective netting are different requirements and should be specified separately.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="finishing"><h2>Hems, eyelets and pockets need an installation plan.</h2><p>Finishing determines how the printed sheet connects to its supports. Reinforced edges, eyelets or pole pockets may be appropriate, depending on the product and location. Agree the proposed system before the artwork is signed off so text and logos stay clear of folds, attachment points and any parts hidden by the frame.</p><p>Do not choose eyelet spacing simply because it was used on the previous banner. A new size, material or position can change the brief. Ask who is responsible for the supports, who will fit the banner and who will inspect it during use. For temporary events, include a practical plan for removal and storage rather than stopping at the opening date.</p><p>A sign on a scaffold or temporary fence requires coordination with the person responsible for that structure. Do not attach advertising without their agreement. The request should include the size, position and proposed material, allowing them to assess the effect on the installation. Mesh should never be presented as automatic approval to cover an otherwise unassessed structure.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="design"><h2>Design for the background and approach.</h2><p>Photograph the site from where the audience will see the banner. A landscape graphic above eye level needs a different composition from a banner beside a queue. Make the business name or event message prominent, then add only the secondary information people genuinely need at that distance. If a web address is included, keep it short and easy to distinguish.</p><p>For mesh, review a printed sample when close-up appearance or brand colour is important. Seeing the actual surface is more useful than judging a small digital mock-up. For solid material, consider reflections and the direction of light. Neither choice makes small text readable from far away, and adding more information usually competes with the main message.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="scenarios"><h2>Three examples of how the brief changes the choice.</h2><p>Illustrative example: a café announces an opening event on a sheltered wall close to the entrance. A solid banner may be a good starting point because the graphics include photography and the audience is nearby. The fitting still needs to suit the wall, and the design should leave space for the agreed attachments.</p><p>Illustrative example: a contractor wants branding on fencing around a Norfolk site. Mesh may be worth assessing, but the fence owner or responsible contractor must first review the proposed covering and supports. A sequence of smaller signs might suit the information hierarchy better than one large continuous graphic. The choice should follow the site assessment, not replace it.</p><p>Illustrative example: an event organiser wants a sponsor backdrop behind speakers indoors. A solid print surface may give cleaner logos, but the system must also fit the venue and its requirements. A banner suspended from an improvised support may be less suitable than a purpose-made display. Start with the available footprint, approved suspension points and presentation photographs.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="permissions"><h2>Check the position before committing to production.</h2><p>Outdoor advertising may need consent even when it is temporary. England’s <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">government advertisement guidance</a> explains the consent framework and advises contacting the relevant local planning authority when requirements are uncertain. Owner permission is also a separate consideration. Confirm the proposed location and display dates before ordering a finished banner.</p><p>For a building wrap or scaffold advertisement, obtain advice on the specific proposal rather than assuming normal small-banner arrangements apply. Supply a photograph and dimensions with your enquiry. We can help organise the signage information, while the relevant authority and people responsible for the site establish the approvals and structural requirements.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="care"><h2>Plan handling, inspection and the next campaign.</h2><p>Agree a safe inspection arrangement appropriate to the display. Look for loose attachments, damaged edges and changes to the supporting structure, following the installer’s instructions. If a banner appears unsafe, keep people clear and involve the responsible installer or site team. Do not climb or attempt repairs without the right arrangements.</p><p>Ask for storage guidance for the exact material and print. Folding, crushing or dragging a graphic can leave marks that detract from a future display. Keep the artwork and dimensions with the banner so a repeat order is straightforward. If dates change each year, consider a design that separates enduring branding from information likely to become obsolete.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Overall dimensions, quantity, display dates and the main message.</li><li>Site photographs showing the background and fixing structure.</li><li>Whether the area is sheltered, exposed or close to passing traffic.</li><li>Who owns and approves the fence, wall, scaffold or frame.</li><li>One-sided or two-sided viewing and the usual viewing distance.</li><li>Existing support details and any venue or contractor specifications.</li><li>Whether supply only, installation, removal or storage advice is needed.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. Answered.</h2><details><summary>Does mesh eliminate wind problems?</summary><p>No. It changes the way air interacts with the banner, but the graphic and its supports still need a suitable specification. The responsible installer or structural specialist should assess the actual arrangement.</p></details><details><summary>Will the colours look identical?</summary><p>Do not assume so. The open surface and background behind mesh affect its appearance. Compare a sample where colour matching matters, particularly when the banner sits alongside solid printed panels.</p></details><details><summary>Can I cut wind slits into a solid banner?</summary><p>Do not modify a finished banner without advice. Cuts can affect the graphic and material behaviour. Discuss the exposure before ordering so the material and fixing system are planned together.</p></details><details><summary>Which is cheaper?</summary><p>Request like-for-like quotations for the same dimensions, artwork and finishing. Installation, access, support work and removal can matter more to the total than the difference between the printable materials.</p></details></section><section class="reading-section" id="sources"><h2>Sources & further reading.</h2><p class="source-note">Sources checked for this draft on 18 October 2026. mainEntity.name: Will the colours look identical?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not assume so. The open surface and background behind mesh affect its appearance. Compare a sample where colour matching matters, particularly when the banner sits alongside solid printed panels.

mainEntity.name: Can I cut wind slits into a solid banner?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not modify a finished banner without advice. Cuts can affect the graphic and material behaviour. Discuss the exposure before ordering so the material and fixing system are planned together.

mainEntity.name: Which is cheaper?

acceptedAnswer.text: Request like-for-like quotations for the same dimensions, artwork and finishing. Installation, access, support work and removal can matter more to the total than the difference between the printable materials.

class="reading-section" id="objective"><h2>Decide what the stand needs to achieve.</h2><p>Before ordering a banner or backdrop, decide what a successful conversation at the event looks like. Are you introducing a new business, demonstrating a product, arranging appointments or collecting enquiries for a particular service? Choose one primary message and one clear next step. This gives the graphics a purpose and helps the team explain the offer consistently throughout the show.</p><p>Think about what visitors see while walking past and what they need once they stop. The main display can identify the business and its offer; smaller material can explain details during a conversation. Avoid putting every service, product and qualification on the largest panel. A focused display leaves room for people and products while making it easier to recognise why your business is relevant.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="booking"><h2>Check the actual booked space and event manual.</h2><p>Obtain your stand number, dimensions and layout from the organiser before choosing hardware. Establish whether the booking is a shell scheme, space-only area, tabletop position or another format. Check which sides are open and what is included. A photograph from last year is a useful reference, but it does not confirm the arrangements for your current booking.</p><p>Read the event’s own exhibitor manual and record its deadlines. Ask about permitted display heights, graphic fixing methods, electrical orders, material documentation and any restrictions relevant to your proposed stand. Requirements can differ between venues and events. Send the relevant instructions to us so the display proposal can be checked against the actual booking rather than a generic exhibition assumption.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="layout"><h2>Draw the stand before buying the pieces.</h2><p>Make a simple plan showing the back wall, open sides, entrance, furniture and any demonstration area. Add the footprint of each proposed display, including its feet or base. A printed width alone does not tell you how much floor space the assembled system occupies. Leave usable space for staff, visitors and conversations, and consider whether a counter or table will obscure the lower part of a graphic.</p><p>Walk through the plan as a visitor. Can someone see the main message from the aisle, approach without feeling blocked and understand where to speak to the team? Think about access for different users and keep the layout straightforward. If you need a particular accessibility arrangement, explain it in the brief and check the venue requirements rather than trying to solve it at the final setup stage.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="choose-display"><h2>Choose displays around transport and repeated use.</h2><p>A pull-up banner may suit a compact presentation or a supporting message. A pop-up backdrop or modular system may be worth discussing for a larger branded area. Choose around the events you expect to attend, the transport available and the people assembling the stand. There is little value in selecting an impressive system that cannot travel with the team or be assembled within the available time.</p><p>Ask for packed dimensions, case information and assembly instructions before deciding. If you already own hardware, send photographs and any model labels. Replacement graphics need to match the actual system, not merely a similar-looking product. Also ask whether future artwork can be changed independently of the hardware and what details you should retain to make repeat ordering straightforward.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="artwork"><h2>Use the correct template for every graphic.</h2><p>Request the production template for the chosen display before preparing artwork. A visible graphic size is not necessarily the complete file size: the system may require allowances, hidden areas or panel divisions. Follow the supplied template and keep important wording away from areas identified as hidden or interrupted. Do not reuse a template from a different stand simply because its advertised width is similar.</p><p>Supply the best available original logo and images, the exact wording and any brand colour references. Tell us if several pieces must look consistent together. Check proofs at a sensible viewing scale, then verify names, telephone numbers, website addresses and offers separately. Test QR codes from the final proof or an appropriate printed test and make sure their destination is ready before the event.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="schedule"><h2>Plan backwards from the date you need to pack.</h2><p>The show opening is not the only deadline. Allow time for approving artwork, production, delivery, inspection and a practice assembly before the team travels. Tell us the date the materials must be with you, not just the date of the event. If the display will go directly to a venue, agree that arrangement explicitly, including the delivery window and the person responsible for receiving it.</p><p>Venue handling rules matter. For example, <a href="https://www.excel.london/exhibitor-manual-content-hub/courier-delivery">Excel London’s courier guidance</a> explains that deliveries are restricted to event tenancy times and that an exhibitor representative or arranged shipping contractor must receive goods; the venue and organiser do not simply accept them on your behalf. Check the current instructions for your own event and pass them to the carrier.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="rehearsal"><h2>Assemble and inspect everything before departure.</h2><p>Open the delivery while there is still time to resolve a problem. Check the printed faces against the approved proof, count the pieces and confirm that the hardware and cases are present. Follow the system’s assembly instructions in a suitable space. A trial setup lets the attending staff become familiar with the display and exposes missing information before they are working under pressure at the venue.</p><p>Photograph the completed arrangement and include the image with the packing list. Label cases clearly with the business name and a contact number, then keep the instructions with the equipment. Record how pieces are packed so that breakdown is as organised as setup. If any hardware is damaged or does not work as expected, contact the supplier rather than forcing it or improvising a repair.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="show-kit"><h2>Prepare a practical show-day kit.</h2><p>Assign someone to own the checklist. Alongside the display, account for approved literature, business cards, product samples, chargers and the equipment needed for your particular demonstration. Confirm any venue-approved arrangements for power and connectivity. Keep the event contacts, delivery booking and assembly instructions available offline, so the team can find them even if mobile reception is poor during setup.</p><p>Plan how enquiries will be recorded and who will follow them up. A clear form or agreed note-taking method helps avoid returning with a stack of business cards and no context. Make the intended follow-up clear to the visitor and use the organisation’s approved process for handling contact information. The graphic should support this conversation with an obvious website, QR code or invitation to speak to the team.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="pack-down"><h2>Include pack-down and the next event in the plan.</h2><p>Check the permitted breakdown time and return transport arrangements in advance. Keep the original cases and protective materials available, and make sure someone knows where they are stored during the show. Pack the display using its instructions, count the components and note damage or missing parts immediately. Store it in conditions appropriate to the product rather than leaving it loose in a vehicle between events.</p><p>After the exhibition, review which messages prompted useful conversations and which pieces were actually used. Keep a photo of the stand, the final artwork, hardware details and a short improvement list together. This record makes the next show easier to prepare and helps you decide whether to update a single graphic, change the layout or add a supporting display. Reuse should be planned, not left to memory.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Event objective, main message and visitor next step agreed.</li><li>Stand number, floor plan, open sides and organiser manual checked.</li><li>Hardware footprint, packed sizes and transport confirmed.</li><li>Correct artwork templates used and final proofs approved.</li><li>Required delivery date, receiving contact and venue slot agreed.</li><li>Full practice assembly completed and photographed.</li><li>Cases labelled, instructions packed and components counted.</li><li>Staff briefed on setup, conversations and enquiry handling.</li><li>Breakdown, return transport and storage planned.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. A pull-up can support a compact message, while a larger display may suit the main visual area. We can discuss the options against your floor plan.</p></details><details><summary>Can you deliver straight to the exhibition venue?</summary><p>Ask when ordering and provide the event manual, receiving contact, stand details and required delivery window. A venue delivery needs an agreed receiving arrangement; it should not be assumed to work like delivery to your normal business address.</p></details><details><summary>When should artwork be ready?</summary><p>Work backwards from the date you need to inspect and pack the display, allowing for proof approval and the agreed production and delivery schedule. Tell us your actual deadline before ordering so feasibility can be confirmed.</p></details></section><section class="reading-section" id="sources"><h2>Sources & further reading.</h2><p class="source-note">Sources checked for this draft on 18 October 2026. href="#services">Explore the services</a></nav></aside><article class="reading-body"><section class="reading-section" id="purpose"><h2>Make the glass apparent before someone reaches it.</h2><p>Glass manifestation is a visible treatment applied to glazing so that people can recognise a door or screen in their path. In an office, showroom or entrance lobby, transparent glass can appear to be an open route. The design task is to make that boundary evident while respecting the use of the space, the available light and the appearance of the building.</p><p>Start with the journey through the room. Walk towards the glazing from the reception desk, corridor, entrance and seating areas. Notice what sits behind it and whether a visitor could mistake a fixed panel for a doorway. Take photographs from both sides. A design selected solely from a flat artwork proof can miss the background and reflections that determine how visible it is.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="england-guidance"><h2>Understand which guidance applies.</h2><p><a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/60d5bdcde90e07716f516cfd/Approved_Document_K.pdf">Approved Document K for England</a> addresses manifestation under requirement K5.2 for relevant non-domestic glazing. Its guidance explains the collision risk, including large uninterrupted transparent screens. It also recognises alternative features that make glazing apparent. Approved Documents describe approaches to meeting requirements; they are not a universal certification for every building or glazing arrangement.</p><p>Existing workplaces also need consideration under workplace health and safety arrangements. <a href="https://www.hse.gov.uk/pubns/books/l24.htm">HSE’s workplace health, safety and welfare guidance</a> is a separate reference for the people managing those premises. For a refurbishment, ask the building designer or relevant building control body to confirm the applicable specification, while the premises manager addresses day-to-day workplace use. The glazing provision appears in <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/3004/regulation/14">regulation 14 of the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992</a>.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="heights"><h2>Set out the two manifestation levels.</h2><p>For the manifestation approach described in Approved Document K, Diagram 7.2 shows two height zones above floor level: 850–1000 mm and 1400–1600 mm. Paragraph 7.4 also describes visual contrast from both sides in all lighting conditions, and minimum heights of 150 mm for logos or signs, or 50 mm for decorative features such as bands. Check the complete <a href="https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/60d5bdcde90e07716f516cfd/Approved_Document_K.pdf">Section 7 guidance and diagrams</a> with your project adviser.</p><p>Record the finished floor level on the survey and proof. If flooring is still being installed, agree who will confirm the final datum before fitting. Do not measure one panel from the skirting and another from an unfinished threshold. A consistent drawing should show the intended position of each marking, its actual height and its relationship to handles, frames and adjoining panels.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="contrast"><h2>Choose the design against the real background.</h2><p>Treat the background as part of the design review. Pale frosting can look distinct against a dark room and much less distinct against a bright window beyond. A strong colour in a brand palette may merge into furniture or a wall on one side. Look at a sample on the actual glass, rather than judging a digital grey background on a laptop.</p><p>For a useful review, photograph the proposed sample from common approaches in daytime and with the usual interior lighting. Include doors in their normal positions and blinds in the positions people actually use. Ask the project adviser to assess the result if the setting is complex. The aim is to select a treatment that works in the occupied room, not merely one that looks elegant in an empty fit-out.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="branding"><h2>Use branding without losing the visual purpose.</h2><p>Manifestation can incorporate company identity, but it needs its own design brief. A repeated logo, a band or a simple pattern should remain recognisable as a treatment across the glazing. Fine outlines and tiny decorative details may be attractive close up while contributing little to the overall effect from a corridor approach. Request a full-size sample where the brand mark has delicate elements.</p><p>Keep promotional information separate where practical. Opening hours, temporary offers and meeting-room names are likely to change at different times from the manifestation. If they are all cut into one large design, replacing a single detail can become unnecessarily complicated. A coordinated system can still look unified while allowing the permanent glass markings to remain intact during routine updates.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="privacy"><h2>Separate privacy from manifestation.</h2><p>Privacy and manifestation can be combined in a carefully specified film layout, but they answer different questions. Privacy concerns what can be seen through the glass. Manifestation concerns whether the glazing itself is evident. Describe both objectives in your enquiry, including whether the space needs privacy at seated height, standing height or only across a particular view.</p><p>For example, a meeting room might need a privacy treatment around the table area and separate consideration of the glazed entrance. A consultation space may need a different arrangement from a showroom where views of the products matter. Do not select a large frosted area merely because it resembles another office; first decide what people inside and outside the room need to see.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="survey"><h2>Create a panel-by-panel survey.</h2><p>Number each door and fixed pane on a simple elevation, then record its width and height. Mark handles, hinges, locks, joints, existing films and any damaged areas. Say which side will receive the graphics and whether furniture or partitions restrict access. A photograph with panel numbers overlaid is especially useful when several meeting rooms have almost identical layouts.</p><p>Give the installer the full glazing arrangement rather than a total square metre figure. Two rooms can have the same glass area but very different cutting and fitting requirements. A continuous run of equal panes is simpler to schedule than many narrow panels, shaped sections and door hardware cut-outs. Accurate panel information also helps order an individual replacement later without reproducing the entire job.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="installation"><h2>Plan fitting around the occupied space.</h2><p>Arrange access so the glass can be cleaned and worked on without people repeatedly moving through the area. Tell the fitting team about opening hours, reception traffic, security procedures and any restrictions on products used inside the premises. If another contractor is still completing decoration or flooring, agree an installation sequence that avoids fresh dust, splashes or changes to the finished level.</p><p>Before applying the full design, confirm the panel references and artwork orientation. A logo intended to be read from reception may be reversed when viewed through the glass if the production method is not clearly specified. Check how the graphics align across door gaps and fixed screens. This coordination is a production task; the project’s responsible adviser should approve the required safety arrangement.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="care"><h2>Keep a record for cleaning and replacement.</h2><p>Ask for care instructions for the specified film and pass them to the cleaning team. Keep the artwork reference, film description and installation date with the panel schedule. When a door is replaced or a screen is moved, the schedule gives the new contractor a starting point and helps identify which part of the design needs to be recreated.</p><p>Include the glass markings in routine premises inspections. Look for lifting edges, missing elements, damage and changes to the surrounding room. New blinds, furniture or wall colours can alter how a treatment appears. When a marking needs replacement, assess the current room as well as matching the old colour; the environment may have changed since the original fit-out.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="next"><h2>Prepare your manifestation enquiry.</h2><p>Send Broadland Digital photographs from both sides, an approximate panel schedule and your preferred visual style. Include the manifestation specification supplied by your designer or building adviser, plus any privacy requirements. If you have no specification yet, say that clearly so the design discussion can identify what needs to be resolved before manufacture.</p><p>Frosted manifestation is the starting service for glass markings; window graphics covers broader branding treatments, and privacy film addresses screening needs. We can discuss the artwork, material and fitting brief around your approved requirements. A completed graphics installation should not be presented as certification of the glazing, the entire building or the wider workplace safety assessment.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Identify every glazed door and screen on a numbered plan.</li><li>Confirm the applicable specification with the project adviser.</li><li>Measure from the finished floor level.</li><li>Review film samples against backgrounds on both sides.</li><li>Separate privacy needs, permanent markings and changing information.</li><li>Keep panel references, artwork and care instructions for future repairs.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. mainEntity.name: Can we use our company logo?

acceptedAnswer.text: A logo can form part of a manifestation design. Its scale, repetition, location and visibility need to work with the approved specification and the actual surroundings.

mainEntity.name: Does any frosted film make the glass compliant?

acceptedAnswer.text: No blanket assurance is possible from the film name alone. The position, design and visibility of the installed treatment need to suit the glazing arrangement and project requirements.

mainEntity.name: Can the graphics be fitted to existing glass?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often the project can be discussed around existing glass, but condition, coatings, previous films and access need checking. Send photographs and details of any existing treatment.

mainEntity.name: What if the floor level changes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Tell the surveyor and installer before final setting out. The approved layout should use the finished floor datum so changes do not silently alter the intended positions.

There is the backing panel or frame, the print or cut lettering, any protective finish, the fixings and the surface they attach to. An illuminated installation also has electrical components. mainEntity.name: Does a seven-year vinyl mean a seven-year guarantee for my whole sign?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. A manufacturer’s material figure is conditional and does not by itself define cover for the finished print, panel, fixings or installation. Ask what the quotation includes and which warranty terms apply to the specified system.

mainEntity.name: Will a laminate make any print suitable for permanent outdoor use?

acceptedAnswer.text: Do not treat lamination as a universal upgrade. The print, film and finish need to be compatible and appropriate for the proposed exposure. We can explain the selected combination when preparing the quote.

mainEntity.name: Can I keep the existing backing panel?

acceptedAnswer.text: Potentially, subject to its condition, surface, fixings and suitability for the new graphics. Photographs are a useful starting point; a closer inspection may be required before reuse can be confirmed.

mainEntity.name: What should I send for an outdoor sign quote?

acceptedAnswer.text: Send the location, approximate dimensions, photographs, your intended message and how long you expect to use it. Tell us about access restrictions and whether you want an existing sign removed or retained.

href="#services">Explore the services</a></nav></aside><article class="reading-body"><section class="reading-section" id="purpose"><h2>You are preparing a quote brief, not a production drawing.</h2><p>The aim of an initial measurement is to help us understand the scale of your shopfront and the sign you want. You do not need a perfect technical drawing to start a conversation. A clear photograph, a labelled sketch and approximate dimensions are usually a better starting point than an unlabelled number with no indication of where it was measured.</p><p>Treat everything you supply at this stage as information for an estimate unless a different arrangement has been explicitly agreed. Final manufacture and installation may require a professional survey. A fascia can look rectangular from the pavement while having awkward returns, uneven edges or hidden supports that affect the finished sign. Mark uncertain dimensions as approximate rather than trying to make them appear precise.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="ground-level"><h2>Keep your initial checks at ground level.</h2><p>Only record dimensions you can obtain safely while standing on the ground in an appropriate place. Do not climb a ladder, stand on furniture, lean from a window or enter a roof to measure the fascia. If the relevant surface cannot be reached safely, send photographs and explain that the dimension needs a survey. Missing information is preferable to an unsafe attempt to collect it.</p><p><a href="https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-at-height/introduction.htm">HSE’s work-at-height guidance</a> prioritises avoiding work at height where practicable and requires appropriate planning, competence and equipment where it is necessary. This customer checklist deliberately stops at safe ground-level observations. It is not a method for accessing elevated signs, removing existing panels or inspecting electrical connections.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="identify"><h2>Identify exactly which area you want to change.</h2><p>Take a straight-on photograph showing the full frontage, then mark the proposed sign area on a copy. Keep the original photograph as well. Label whether you mean the existing printed face, the full fascia band, a new panel over part of that band or individual letters fixed directly to the background. Those are different proposals even if they occupy a similar position.</p><p>If the frontage contains several panels, number them from left to right when viewed from outside. If it wraps around a corner, label the front and side separately. State whether the new design should cover the whole arrangement or only a particular panel. This simple naming system helps the quote, artwork discussion and eventual survey refer to the same parts of the building.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="dimensions"><h2>Label width, height and any known projections.</h2><p>Write dimensions in millimetres and use width × height in that order. State what the figures describe. For example, an illustrative note might read: existing sign face approximately 4200 mm wide × 650 mm high, estimated from available ground-level information, survey required. That is much more useful than writing 4.2 × 0.65 without units or a description of the surface.</p><p>If you already have reliable building drawings or a previous sign drawing, send them and identify their date. Do not assume an old drawing still matches the frontage. Where a dimension cannot be checked safely, leave it blank or mark it unknown. Do not infer manufacturing dimensions from a photograph, count bricks as a precise scale or round a rough estimate into a supposedly exact measurement.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="photo-pack"><h2>Send a small, well-chosen set of photographs.</h2><p>Start with a full-frontage image taken as square to the building as practical. Add a wider street view showing the entrance and neighbouring features, followed by left and right oblique views. Use your phone’s normal camera view where possible and send the original files. A heavily cropped screenshot can hide the very information needed to understand the edges of the fascia.</p><p>From safe public or authorised ground-level positions, photograph any visible obstruction: a canopy, shutter housing, downpipe, alarm box, camera or light fitting. Take close views only where they can be obtained without climbing or reaching into an unsafe area. Explain what each photograph shows. If the sign is illuminated, a normal evening photograph can help explain the desired appearance, but do not open any equipment.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="existing"><h2>Describe the existing fascia without dismantling it.</h2><p>Tell us whether you want the current sign removed, covered, refreshed or assessed for reuse. Say what you know about its material and age, and be clear when you are guessing. If you have an invoice, drawing or maintenance record, it may help identify the existing construction. An accessible photograph is useful; taking a panel off to look behind it is not part of this initial checklist.</p><p>Note visible damage or areas where the surface looks uneven. Photograph the concern and leave investigation to the survey. If there are cables, existing lights or an illuminated sign box, identify them in the brief so the installation scope can include the appropriate specialist arrangements. Do not disconnect, modify or test electrical equipment to make a quote enquiry more complete.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="access"><h2>Show how the fitting team would reach the frontage.</h2><p>The sign dimensions are only part of the installation price. Explain what is below the fascia: a pavement, steps, parked cars, planting, a forecourt or a narrow doorway. State whether there are delivery hours, shared access arrangements or busy customer periods. Photographs should show the immediate working area so that access can be considered during the survey rather than after manufacture.</p><p>Include the site address and postcode, a contact person and any landlord or managing-agent requirements you already have. If work must happen outside your opening hours, say so early. Do not promise that a particular access method will fit merely because another contractor used it previously. The fitting arrangement will need to suit this job and the conditions at the time.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="design-brief"><h2>Add the information that shapes the design.</h2><p>Send your logo in the best available original format, the exact business name and the wording you want on the sign. Identify the main message and the information that is optional. A fascia does not need to reproduce every line from your website. Tell us where customers will first see it and whether the priority is recognition from the road, reassurance at the entrance or visibility after dark.</p><p>If you have a preferred sign style, attach a reference and explain what you like: flat panels, individual letters, colour, depth or a particular finish. A reference image is a design starting point, not evidence that the same construction suits your building. If illumination is being considered, state the requirement so availability, specification and installation arrangements can be discussed before the design develops.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="next-step"><h2>What happens after you send the measurements?</h2><p>We can review the brief, clarify the intended sign and discuss an initial specification. The next step may be an indicative estimate, a request for another photograph or a site survey. Confirm whether a quoted figure is provisional and what information remains outstanding. That keeps the budget discussion useful while avoiding the impression that a rough customer measurement has been accepted for manufacture.</p><p>Before production, make sure the final size, wording, colours, construction and installation scope are agreed. Check the artwork proof carefully, including contact details and any directional information. Approval of the visual design should be clearly distinguished from responsibility for final site dimensions. If your opening date is fixed, tell us at the start so the required checks and approvals can be scheduled around it.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Full site address, postcode and contact details.</li><li>Original front, side and wider context photographs.</li><li>Numbered sketch identifying each sign face or return.</li><li>Width × height in millimetres, with estimates clearly labelled.</li><li>Existing sign removal or reuse preference.</li><li>Logo, exact wording, preferred style and target date.</li><li>Access restrictions, opening hours and landlord requirements.</li><li>Unknown dimensions listed for professional survey.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. Answered.</h2><details><summary>Can you quote if I cannot reach the fascia?</summary><p>Send photographs and any existing drawings, and explain which measurements are unknown. We can discuss an initial estimate or arrange the next step without asking you to work at height.</p></details><details><summary>Should I measure the panel or the whole frontage?</summary><p>Identify both if you already have safe, reliable information, and label them separately. The important point is to show which area the proposed sign will occupy. Do not assume the existing panel fills the entire available fascia.</p></details><details><summary>Can a phone photo provide the final dimensions?</summary><p>A photograph helps explain the site, but it should not be treated as a reliable manufacturing measurement on its own. Perspective and lens effects can change apparent proportions. Final dimensions need an agreed verification method.</p></details><details><summary>Do I need to remove the old sign before asking for a quote?</summary><p>No. Send the information available without dismantling it. Removal, assessment of the background and any making-good work can then be considered as part of the agreed project scope.</p></details></section><section class="reading-section" id="sources"><h2>Sources & further reading.</h2><p class="source-note">Sources checked for this draft on 18 October 2026. Product ratings apply to the stated product and test conditions; confirm the current specification for your order.</p><ul class="source-links"><li><a class="" href="https://www.hse.gov.uk/work-at-height/introduction.htm">HSE: introduction to working at height safely ↗</a></li></ul></section><section class="reading-section" id="services"><h2>Put the advice into practice.</h2><p>Tell us where the sign will go, what it needs to communicate and the date you are working towards. Our Norwich team can discuss the design, materials and fitting around your project.</p><div class="service-links"><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs/fascia-signs">Fascia signs ↗</a><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs/built-up-3d-letters">Built-up 3D letters ↗</a></div><p><a class="" href="/signage-home/signage-norwich">Visit our Norwich workshop ↗</a> · <a class="" href="/sectors">Find signage for your sector ↗</a></p></section></article></div><section class="section tint"><div class="wrap"><h2>A little more guidance.</h2><div class="grid research-cards"><article class="card" data-search="Do you need planning consent for a shop sign? A flat fascia, individual letters, a projecting sign and a lit display can create very different schemes, even when they carry the same business name. Gather a photograph of the whole frontage and a simple description before asking anyone to judge whether approval is needed.</p><p>In England, advertisements have their own consent process within the planning system. Some fall outside the need for deemed or express consent, some have deemed consent subject to conditions, and others need express consent. The position depends on the complete proposal. <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">Government guidance on advertisements</a> explains the three routes and recommends contacting the local planning authority where the answer is uncertain.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="permissions"><h2>Separate the different permissions.</h2><p>Advertisement consent, landlord approval and listed building consent are different checks. Having one does not automatically provide the others. Government guidance also explains how planning permission relates to displaying an advertisement, and why separate building alterations need consideration. <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">Read the consent and ownership guidance</a> before treating an existing shopfront as permission for every proposed change. The governing legislation is the <a href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/783/contents">Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) (England) Regulations 2007, as amended</a>.</p><p>For a rented unit, begin with your lease and the managing agent. Ask who can approve the sign, whether the building has a signage manual and whether fixing into the frontage is permitted. A retail park may want consistent panel sizes; a shared building may control tenant names; an older frontage may have details that the landlord wants retained. Capture those instructions in writing and send them with the design brief.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="describe"><h2>Describe the complete proposal.</h2><p>Give the council and your designer the same set of information. A request described only as a new logo leaves too much unclear. Explain the overall panel width and height, the depth of lettering, the position above the pavement, the projection from the wall and the intended finish. Include every element you are changing, rather than discussing the fascia while leaving a separate blade sign until installation week.</p><p>For lighting, identify whether the sign itself glows or whether external fittings illuminate it. Include the proposed colour, operating hours and the manufacturer information available for the lighting. Do not substitute a brightened photograph for a technical description. An image can communicate appearance, while drawings and specifications explain what will actually be fitted.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="context"><h2>Show the frontage in its street setting.</h2><p>Take one straight-on photograph and several wider views from normal approaches. Include the upper floors and neighbouring units, because a close crop can hide the features that influence a design. Note whether pedestrians approach from an angle, whether a bus stop interrupts the sightline and whether the entrance is recessed. These observations help create a sign that can be read without simply making it larger.</p><p>The advertisement regime considers amenity and public safety. <a href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">Government advertisement guidance</a> also notes that other statutory provisions can apply, including listed building consent. For a sensitive site, ask the authority which local design guidance and permissions relate to the property; avoid assuming that a sign seen elsewhere in the same street establishes what is acceptable for yours.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="existing"><h2>Treat replacement signs as a fresh check.</h2><p>An existing sign is useful survey information, but it is not a complete approval file. Photograph it, measure it where safe and ask the owner for the original drawings and decision documents. Record which parts you intend to keep. Replacing only the face of a sound panel is a different production brief from removing the whole assembly and introducing deep lettering, new brackets or illumination.</p><p>Compare the old and proposed schemes side by side. Use a short change list: wording, colours, dimensions, position, construction and lighting. Send that list when requesting advice so the response addresses the change you intend to make. If documents cannot be found, say so plainly. This is more useful than describing a substantially altered display as a like-for-like replacement.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="application-pack"><h2>Build one clear drawing pack.</h2><p>Create a project folder with the site address, your contact details, ownership contact, dated photos, measured elevations and artwork. Number the drawings and give each revision a date. A useful elevation shows the whole shopfront with the proposed sign accurately positioned, rather than an isolated rectangle with a logo. Keep the business name consistent across the application, artwork proof and quotation.</p><p>Ask the relevant authority for its application requirements and validation checklist. If you appoint a planning professional, agree who prepares drawings, submits the application and answers queries. Ask your sign maker which production details they can supply. This division of work should be explicit; ordering a sign does not mean an application has been submitted on your behalf.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="design"><h2>Use the approval process to improve the design.</h2><p>Start with a readable business name and a simple message hierarchy. A fascia does not need to reproduce every line of your website. Put the most important identification where it can be seen clearly, then decide whether opening hours or supporting services belong on the window. A restrained arrangement often gives individual elements more room and makes future updates easier.</p><p>Consider how the proposal works with the architecture. Align the sign with the available fascia space, show where fixings will sit and avoid concealing features without a clear reason. Prepare an alternative finish or layout where the initial idea depends on an uncertain feature. Having a considered second option can make a discussion more productive than redesigning the whole scheme at the last moment.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="programme"><h2>Allow time between design, approval and fitting.</h2><p>Work backwards from your opening date, leaving separate stages for the survey, concept, any consent process, final artwork, manufacture and installation. Do not book a launch around a production date that assumes every preceding decision is already resolved. If the frontage is being refurbished, coordinate with the contractor so final measurements reflect the finished surface rather than a temporary opening.</p><p>Before production, assemble a release pack containing the final approved drawing, relevant decision and conditions, landlord permission and the signed artwork proof. Ask who will check that the manufactured sign matches this pack. If something changes after approval, such as a deeper casing or another light fitting, pause and check the effect before treating it as a minor workshop substitution.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="example"><h2>Example: a new occupier taking over a shop.</h2><p>Imagine a café moving into a unit with an old non-illuminated fascia. The owner initially wants a new panel, then adds a projecting sign and lighting. A useful brief lists all three items from the outset, with photographs and approximate dimensions. The landlord supplies the existing signage rules, and the business asks the council about the complete proposal before approving production artwork.</p><p>The design can then distinguish permanent identification from changing offers. The fascia carries the café name; the window carries opening hours; promotions use a separate display area. This is an illustrative planning workflow, not a statement that any particular café proposal will be approved. Its value is that everyone works from the same scheme and knows which decisions remain open.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="next"><h2>Turn the agreed design into a sign specification.</h2><p>Once the approval route is established, the production brief can focus on materials, colours, fixing arrangements and access. Send Broadland Digital your address, frontage photographs, dimensions and any permission documents. Tell us whether you are keeping an existing panel or replacing the structure, and flag any date that depends on another contractor finishing first.</p><p>Explore shop and building signs for the overall scheme, then discuss fascia or projecting signs for the individual elements. The quotation should make clear what design, survey and fitting work is included. Keep the consent record with the final proof so future changes start from a useful reference rather than another search through old emails.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="checklist"><h2>Your project checklist.</h2><ul class="project-checklist"><li>Photograph the complete frontage and street approaches.</li><li>List every sign, its dimensions, position and illumination.</li><li>Check ownership permission and any building signage rules.</li><li>Ask the local planning authority about the exact proposal.</li><li>Keep dated drawings, decisions and conditions together.</li><li>Release production only against the agreed final specification.</li></ul><p><a class="button purple" href="#enquiry">TALK THROUGH YOUR PROJECT ↗</a></p></section><section class="reading-section" id="faq"><h2>Your questions. Answered.</h2><details><summary>Does every shop sign need an application?</summary><p>No. The route depends on the advertisement and its conditions. Ask the local planning authority to assess your specific proposal rather than applying a blanket rule based only on size.</p></details><details><summary>Can I use the previous tenant’s permission?</summary><p>Retrieve the decision and drawings, then compare them with your proposed scheme. Ask the authority whether the changes are covered before relying on the previous display.</p></details><details><summary>Can you quote before permission is resolved?</summary><p>An initial quotation can help establish a budget, provided the assumptions are recorded. Production should follow the final agreed dimensions, construction and approval requirements.</p></details><details><summary>What should I send with an enquiry?</summary><p>Send the address, photographs, approximate dimensions, preferred sign style and any landlord or council correspondence. Tell us which items are confirmed and which remain proposals.</p></details></section><section class="reading-section" id="sources"><h2>Sources & further reading.</h2><p class="source-note">Sources checked for this draft on 18 October 2026. Product ratings apply to the stated product and test conditions; confirm the current specification for your order.</p><ul class="source-links"><li><a class="" href="https://www.gov.uk/guidance/advertisements">GOV.UK: Advertisements — England planning guidance ↗</a></li><li><a class="" href="https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2007/783/contents">Town and Country Planning (Control of Advertisements) (England) Regulations 2007 ↗</a></li></ul><p class="source-note">This guide concerns England. The relevant authority or responsible project team should confirm the requirements for your premises. Technical production review is required before public launch.</p></section><section class="reading-section" id="services"><h2>Put the advice into practice.</h2><p>Tell us where the sign will go, what it needs to communicate and the date you are working towards. Our Norwich team can discuss the design, materials and fitting around your project.</p><div class="service-links"><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs">Shop and building signs ↗</a><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs/fascia-signs">Fascia signs ↗</a><a class="button" href="/signage-home/building-signage-shop-signs/projecting-signs">Projecting signs ↗</a></div><p><a class="" href="/signage-home/signage-norwich">Visit our Norwich workshop ↗</a> · <a class="" href="/sectors">Find signage for your sector ↗</a></p></section></article></div><section class="section tint"><div class="wrap"><h2>A little more guidance.</h2><div class="grid research-cards"><article class="card" data-search="How to measure a fascia for a sign quote Send useful ground-level measurements and photographs for an initial shop sign quotation. Learn what to label, which views help and which dimensions must wait for a professional survey."><a href="/signage-home/guides-and-advice/how-to-measure-a-fascia"><img alt="How to measure a fascia for a sign quote — signage example" height="900" loading="lazy" src="https://dipjypzrfigkzuarlsov.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/seo-images/ae4393de-99e2-4a0f-be28-2866e44443bd/signage/research/how-to-measure-a-fascia.webp" width="1600"/><h3>How to measure a fascia for a sign quote ↗</h3></a><p>Send useful ground-level measurements and photographs for an initial shop sign quotation. Learn what to label, which views help and which dimensions must wait for a professional survey.</p></article><article class="card" data-search="How long do outdoor signs last? An outdoor sign is a combination of panel, graphics, fixings and installation. Here is how to choose a sensible specification, understand durability figures and plan for maintenance or a future refresh."><a href="/signage-home/guides-and-advice/how-long-do-outdoor-signs-last"><img alt="How long do outdoor signs last? — signage example" height="900" loading="lazy" src="https://dipjypzrfigkzuarlsov.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/seo-images/ae4393de-99e2-4a0f-be28-2866e44443bd/signage/research/how-long-do-outdoor-signs-last.webp" width="1600"/><h3>How long do outdoor signs last? ↗</h3></a><p>An outdoor sign is a combination of panel, graphics, fixings and installation. Here is how to choose a sensible specification, understand durability figures and plan for maintenance or a future refresh.</p></article><article class="card" data-search="Foamex vs aluminium composite vs Correx Choose a board around its setting, support and useful working life. Compare rigid PVC, aluminium composite and fluted polypropylene for indoor displays, outdoor branding and temporary site information."><a href="/signage-home/compare/foamex-vs-aluminium-composite-vs-correx"><img alt="Foamex vs aluminium composite vs Correx — signage example" height="900" loading="lazy" src="https://dipjypzrfigkzuarlsov.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/seo-images/ae4393de-99e2-4a0f-be28-2866e44443bd/signage/research/foamex-vs-aluminium-composite-vs-correx.webp" width="1600"/><h3>Foamex vs aluminium composite vs Correx ↗</h3></a><p>Choose a board around its setting, support and useful working life.
